1.pericope_label: I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse... I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the difficulty of the opening invitation to lie in what is drunk, and the margin to settle it — the new strong wine of love and not the fruit of the grape, the poet inviting others into sympathy with his joy, for which he quotes Shelley. At the second verse he states the dream reading outright: the poet pictures his lady dreaming, the realities that hindered their union reappearing in the fancies of sleep, so that when the seeming hindrance is withdrawn she finds him gone; he compares the shut-out lover cold with the dews of midnight to a Greek lyric, and glosses the garment of the third verse as a tunic. Delitzsch reads the first verse as the union of love completing a betrothal, the God-ordained end of such love within the limits morality fixes, and fills in the third from the words themselves — she lies unclothed, and the washing implies she had gone barefoot through the day — distinguishing the Hebrew word for the linen garment from the Arabic for cotton.

Gill thinks the first verse should have closed the previous chapter, being Christ's answer to the church's request. He is careful about the sleep: not the dead sleep of sin, not a judicial slumber, but a frame unbecoming a saint, consistent with grace though grace is then little in exercise. He turns the excuses of the third verse into the language of backsliding, the coat being the conversation she failed to keep and the unwillingness to rise an unwillingness to leave carnal ease for the trials that following him would bring.

Clarke wants the opening verb in the past tense and the previous chapter's last clause carried down, reads the closing invitation as the bridegroom's words to his companions after the nuptial chamber when the customary proofs of the bride's purity had been shown, and rejects the reading that gives those words to the bride since the verbs are plural. He doubts whether the passage down to the seventh verse is anything but a dream, finding that supposition solves what is otherwise awkward, and says the bride must have been dreaming or in real disorder of mind to make excuses so frivolous, adding a traveller's report of the same excuse still made where floors are of earth. Wesley hears Christ knocking by his word and providence and Spirit at the door of the heart and takes the dew for what he suffered for the church, while reading the excuses plainly as those of someone already settled for the night.

Henry makes the answer outdo the request: she called him her beloved and he calls her his sister and spouse; she called the garden his and he owns it, though of small account, which Henry sets against the times when God disowned Israel and called their feasts theirs rather than his. On the sleep he traces a decline — affections cooled, duty neglected, ease indulged — and observes that this sometimes follows more than ordinary enlargements, since even Paul was in danger of being puffed up by abundant revelations.

debates.question: Is the night scene a dream or a real declension?

positions.view: Probably a dream throughout, down to the seventh verse; the supposition resolves her hesitation, his sudden disappearance, and her being abroad in such disorder that the watch might take her for a suspicious person.
A dream, and deliberately so: the poet pictures his lady dreaming, and the hindrances to their union reappear in the fancies of sleep.
A real declension: not the dead sleep of sin nor a judicial slumber, but a frame unbecoming a saint in which grace is little in exercise.

debates.question: Who speaks the closing invitation of the first verse, and what is drunk?

positions.view: The bridegroom, to his companions, after the nuptial chamber and the customary proofs of the bride's purity; the reading that gives the words to the bride fails because the verbs are plural.
Not a marriage feast at all: what is drunk is the new strong wine of love, the poet inviting others into sympathy with his joy.
Christ, delighting in the obedience of his people and bidding believers eat their spiritual food freely.
The words mark the union of love that completes a betrothal, the God-ordained end of such love within the limits morality fixes.

outliers.note: Quotes Shelley to catch the feeling of the opening invitation, and a Greek lyric for the shut-out lover standing cold and wet with the dews of midnight.

Supports the second excuse with a contemporary traveller's report that the same objection — that rising would dirty the washed feet — is still made where floors are of earth and shoes are not worn indoors.

themes: I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.

I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.
I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?

4.pericope_label: My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him... The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the fullest account of the lock: a hollow bolt through a staple into the door-post, with movable pins dropping into matching holes, opened by a key slid inside the bolt, or by an arm worked in and the pins pushed up by a hand carrying something soft. From this he explains the myrrh — the lover, lacking a key, uses the gift he brought to try the lock, fails, and leaves the scent on the handle. He supposes an exclamation of disappointment from the departing lover, and identifies the lost garment as a light wrap thrown on for going out in haste. Delitzsch derives the word for the opening from a root meaning to break through and places it above the bolt, distinguishes the myrrh that flows of itself, describes the sinking of the soul that is not the ecstasy of love, keeps the watchmen a literal patrol who struck the king's own bride as a common woman, turns her searching in the city rather than the fields into an argument against the shepherd theory, and states plainly at the close that all of it was dreamed.

Gill makes the door the heart and the crevice a sign that it was not wholly shut, the hand being efficacious grace; he has the church, once opened, patent to Christ alone, and at the close humbling herself to ask the help of weaker believers in the search.

Clarke allows that if the scene were real the language would carry its married sense, but repeats that it bears every evidence of a dream; he explains the myrrh from the Roman custom of anointing the bridegroom's door-posts, from which he derives the Latin word for a wife, reports that tearing a woman's veil is Eastern speech for dishonouring her, and marks the end of the third day and night at the charge. Wesley makes the hand the finger of God working on the conscience, reads the withdrawal as just punishment for earlier neglect, and takes the watchmen for the governors of the church, bound to comfort the faithful and discouraging them instead.

debates.question: What is the hand put in by the opening?

positions.view: A literal attempt on a literal lock, whose mechanism explains the myrrh left on the handle when the attempt failed.
Literal, the aperture pierced in the door above the bolt, named from a root meaning to break through.
If the scene were real the language would carry its married sense; but it is most likely a dream.
Efficacious grace, the finger of God, working inwardly on a conscience whose door was not entirely shut.

debates.question: Who are the watchmen, and what does the beating mean?

positions.view: A real city patrol, rough men judging by externals who struck the king's own bride as they would any common woman found abroad at night.
Real, and the tearing of the veil carries its Eastern sense of dishonouring a woman.
The governors of the church, bound to comfort the faithful and frequently discouraging them, whose stripping of the veil denies her relation to Christ.
Not identified; the interest is in the garment, a light wrap thrown on for going out in haste and named once elsewhere.

outliers.note: Reconstructs the ancient Palestinian pin-lock in detail and uses the mechanism itself to explain the myrrh on the handle: the lover, having no key, tried the pins with the perfume he had brought as a gift.
Turns the detail that she searched in the city rather than in the open field or the villages into an argument against the theory that the beloved of the Song is a shepherd.

themes: My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him.
I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.
I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.
The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.

9.pericope_label: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women?... My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand

schools.summary: Ellicott puts the question of the ninth verse to a use none of the others make: since love-poems describe the charms of the one addressed but not of the poet himself, a passage describing the bridegroom makes it nearly certain the poem was sung as a wedding-song by alternating voices of maidens and young men, as in the marriage poem of Catullus. He notes the margin at the tenth verse, gives the curls two derivations, reports that the Greek and Latin versions read the word differently and rendered palm-leaves, and on the eyes reports the received explanation — a jewel set in a ring's foil — while preferring to keep the bird bathing, quoting Keats and an Indian poem. Delitzsch holds the question cannot proceed from ignorance but exists to give her occasion to praise him, answers the charge that the eulogy is intolerable self-praise if Solomon wrote it by observing that the words are Shulamith's and that love idealizes, distinguishes the two words for gold, and takes the moist glancing of the eye for doves sipping beside a watercourse.

Gill takes the two colours for the two natures, citing Cicero that a colour without mixture is chiefly becoming to God, while allowing that both may belong to the manhood. On the head he collects rather than decides, some understanding a diadem and others the hair powdered with gold dust in the manner Josephus records of the youths attending Solomon; and he reads the eyes as omniscience turned toward his people in mercy, not fierce but lovely.

Clarke says the question gives the bride her opening, keeps the description to complexion, reads the following phrase literally as bearing the standard among ten thousand, suggests the crisped hair may be the moustache, and explains the whiteness of the eye by the eastern use of a dark cosmetic which gives such lustre that a traveller said they seem to be swimming in bliss. Wesley agrees on the colours but then enters a protest reaching the whole passage: we need not aim at a distinct application of these particulars to some special excellency of Christ, since such things are mere conjectures, the design being only to set him forth as one in whom there is no blemish from crown to sole.

Henry reports a harsher reading of the question, that some take it as blame for making such ado about him, but dwells rather on the beauty that even slight acquaintance with Christ can see in those who bear his image.

debates.question: Should the particulars of the description be given distinct spiritual meanings?

positions.view: No — such applications are mere conjectures; the design is only to set him forth as one in whom there is no blemish from crown to sole.
Yes, and each detail is worked: the colours for the two natures, the eyes for omniscience turned toward his people in mercy.
The description is of a person, and the questions it raises are of language and custom rather than of application.
Neither pressed nor refused; the interest lies in what the daughters' question shows about the church's beauty.

debates.question: In what spirit do the daughters ask their question?

positions.view: Sincerely — not scornfully, not to shift off the trouble laid on them, and not in total ignorance, but wanting to hear more.
It cannot proceed from ignorance; it exists to give her occasion to praise him aloud.
Some take it as blame for making such ado about him.
As a device: it gives the bride her opening for the description that follows.
As evidence of performance — that the poem was sung antiphonally by choirs of maidens and young men.

outliers.note: Argues from the mere existence of a description of the bridegroom that the poem must have been performed antiphonally, since love-poems praise the one addressed and not the poet, comparing the marriage poem of Catullus.

Answers the objection that the eulogy would be intolerable self-praise on Solomon's part by observing that he does not say it of himself but puts it in Shulamith's mouth, and that love idealizes — she sees him in her own transforming light.

themes: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?
My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand.
His head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven.
His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, and fitly set.

13.pericope_label: His cheeks are as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers... His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Ellicott agrees the cheeks are probably a perfumed beard and notes the margin's towers of perfumes, quotes Tennyson on the lips, reads the word rendered rings as a cylinder referring to the rounded arm, suggests stones of Tarshish — chrysolite or topaz, said to have been first found in an ancient city of Spain — and insists with Delitzsch that the last verse names the palate as the organ of speech. Delitzsch keeps the cheeks to the face itself, the word for the bed coming from a root meaning to slope and the comparison lying in the soft elevation; he rejects the lexicons' account of the hands as a closed fist whose stained nails are the gems, since it is nowhere shown that Israelites stained their nails and the word means the outstretched hand; he states at the legs the principle that living beauty rendered in words must borrow its figures from dead matter and so must always come short, while noting that the feet are in fact the pedestal of the bony pillars of the legs; and he rejects as fanciful the reading of the last verse as a mouth for kissing.

Gill reports the beard reading from a Jewish commentator and many Christian ones while offering the cheek as the seat of blushing and so of Christ's humility. He keeps the rings literal, notes that the stone was worn on the fingers and stood in the high priest's breastplate, and collects the candidates for it — the best beryl resembling the colour of the sea, or chrysolite, or the jacinth. At the legs he looks for the sense in dress, either the priestly linen garments of thread six times doubled, stiff and white as marble, or the eastern sandal bound with golden ribbons. At the last verse he will not choose among the senses, offering the words of the Gospel, the kisses of his mouth, the voice, and a rendering as taste.

Clarke defends the beard at length, holding that scarcely anything sets off a face better when kept in order and reporting women who not only despised but execrated close-shaved Europeans; he prefers chrysolite for the stone, decides the clause about the body must mean a jewelled garment since the literal sense is plain enough but hardly intended, takes the golden sockets for slippers such as still receive lavish ornament in Asia, and describes the close as a collapse of language, her metaphors exhausted until she can only say the whole of him is loveliness. Wesley compares the feet to fine brass for their brightness and glosses the summary in four words as a refusal to run out into more particulars.

positions.view: Yes, and the thing is worth defending: kept in order it sets off a face better than almost anything.
Probably, the allusion being to a beard perfumed.
So a Jewish commentator and many Christian ones read it, though the cheek as the seat of blushing yields Christ's humility.
No — the face itself, the comparison lying in the soft elevation of the cheek and the refreshing impression it makes.
The countenance generally, of which the cheeks are an eminent part.

debates.question: What are the hands compared to?

positions.view: Not a closed fist with stained nails for gems, as the lexicons have it, but the outstretched hand, the word meaning a cylinder rather than a ring.
A cylinder likewise, referring to the rounded arm.
Literal rings set with stones, with bracelets at the wrists.
Literal rings, the stone being one worn on the fingers and set in the high priest's breastplate.
Adornment simply — beautiful and precious, as with gold rings set with stones.

outliers.note: Turns the comment on the cheeks into a defence of beards, reporting that he has known women who not only despised but execrated close-shaved Europeans.

States at the legs a general principle for the whole description: living beauty rendered in words rather than colours must borrow its figures from minerals and plants, and every such comparison must come short, because dead matter cannot fairly represent what is alive.

themes: His cheeks are as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers: his lips like lilies, dropping sweet smelling myrrh.
His hands are as gold rings set with the beryl: his belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires.
His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.
His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
